function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
**Triangulation Metrics** is a set of quantitative measures used to evaluate the quality and reliability of triangulation results in geospatial analysis. Triangulation, in this context, refers to the process of determining the position of a point by measuring angles from known points at either end of a fixed baseline. The metrics help assess how well the triangulation has performed and whether the derived coordinates meet required accuracy standards.

Key aspects typically covered by triangulation metrics include:

| Metric | What it Measures | Typical Use |
|--------|------------------|-------------|
| **Baseline Length** | Distance between the two known points used for triangulation. | Longer baselines can improve precision but may introduce more error if the baseline isn’t accurately measured. |
| **Angle Accuracy** | Precision of the angle measurements taken from each known point. | Small angular errors can lead to significant positional errors, especially over long distances. |
| **Baseline Error** | Uncertainty in the measurement of the baseline itself. | Baseline errors propagate into the final coordinate estimates. |
| **Coordinate Uncertainty** | Estimated standard deviation or confidence interval for the computed coordinates. | Provides a statistical measure of how reliable the derived position is. |
| **Residuals** | Difference between observed and calculated angles or distances. | Helps identify systematic errors or outliers in the data. |
| **Redundancy** | Number of observations per unknown. | Higher redundancy generally improves the reliability of the solution. |
| **Weighting Factors** | Relative importance assigned to different observations based on their expected accuracy. | Allows the algorithm to give more influence to higher‑quality data. |
| **Error Propagation** | How measurement errors combine to affect the final result. | Used to estimate overall uncertainty and to design better observation strategies. |

In practice, triangulation metrics are often computed automatically by surveying software or GIS tools when you run a triangulation analysis. They provide a quick snapshot of the solution’s quality and help you decide whether additional observations or corrections are needed before using the derived coordinates for critical applications such as mapping, construction, or scientific research.
